title: Close Ties
goals: Talk about friendships and relationships with precise vocabulary (confidant, close-knit, drift apart).
Give extra, precise information with relative clauses (non-defining, whose, where, which, preposition + whom).
Shorten sentences with reduced clauses (the woman sitting next to me; a message sent by my ex).
Use separable and inseparable phrasal verbs when talking about relationships (let down, put up with, fall out with).
Talk about two people with both, neither, either and each other.
Soften criticism and opinions so you sound natural and kind (a bit, kind of, I guess, though).

words.example: He isn't a friend, just an acquaintance from the gym.
We're a close-knit group, so we see each other every week.
Rosa and I have been lifelong friends since primary school.
My sister is my closest confidant; I tell her everything.
A colleague recommended this restaurant to me.

We were rivals at school, but now we get on well.

Her circle of friends is small but very loyal.

learn.title: Relative clauses: non-defining, whose and where
learn.html:
You already know the relative clauses that identify a person (the friend who lives next door). At B2 we add those that give extra information and those that use whose, where and which referring to a whole idea.

TypeExampleKey points
Defining (necessary)The friend (who / that) I trust most is Ana.No commas; that can be used; the object pronoun can be left out.
Non-defining (extra)My oldest friend, who lives in Quito, is visiting.Between commas; NEVER that; the pronoun is not left out.
whose + nounI have a colleague whose brother is a famous chef.Possession (belonging to someone); no article after it.
where / whenThat's the café where we first met.Place and time.
which = the whole previous ideaHe never replies, which really annoys me.Commas; which refers to the whole sentence.
PrepositionThe friend I grew up with / The friend with whom I grew up.Informal: preposition at the end. Formal: preposition + whom / which (never that).

Remember: in English the pronoun is not repeated inside the relative clause: The man I met, not The man I met him.

watch.wrong: My sister, that lives in Monterrey, is a nurse.
watch.right: My sister, who lives in Monterrey, is a nurse.
watch.why: In non-defining clauses (with commas), that is not used.

watch.wrong: The man who I talked to him is Pablo.
watch.right: The man who I talked to is Pablo. / The man I talked to is Pablo.
watch.why: Don't repeat the pronoun: who already replaces him.

watch.wrong: I have a friend which parents are doctors.
watch.right: I have a friend whose parents are doctors.

watch.wrong: The friend with who I travel is funny.
watch.right: The friend with whom I travel is funny.

learn.title: Reduced clauses with -ing and -ed
learn.html:
In written and natural spoken English you can shorten a relative clause when the pronoun is the subject: drop who / which / that and the verb be.

Full formReducedRule
The woman who is sitting next to me is my aunt.The woman sitting next to me is my aunt.Active voice → verb with -ing.
People who live nearby can walk to school.People living nearby can walk to school.Simple present → -ing.
A message that was sent by my ex made me sad.A message sent by my ex made me sad.Passive voice → past participle (-ed / 3rd form).
The guests who were invited came early.The guests invited came early.Drop who + was/were.
  • You only reduce if the pronoun is the subject. In The friend (that) I met the pronoun is an object: there is no reduced form.
  • For a single completed action in the past, don't use -ing: The man who called yesterday is not the man calling yesterday.

watch.wrong: The woman who sitting there is my cousin.
watch.right: The woman sitting there is my cousin.
watch.why: Either the full relative clause (who is sitting) or the reduced one (sitting), but don't mix them.

watch.wrong: The book writing by my friend is a bestseller.
watch.right: The book written by my friend is a bestseller.

watch.wrong: The people invite to the party were late.
watch.right: The people invited to the party were late.

watch.wrong: The man calling you yesterday is my boss.
watch.right: The man who called you yesterday is my boss.
watch.why: A single completed past action is not reduced with -ing.

My parents were very supportive when I changed careers.

learn.title: Phrasal verbs: separable, inseparable and three-part
learn.html:
A phrasal verb is a verb + particle (up, out, down, with…). The verb is conjugated; the particle does not change. Three groups:

GroupExamplesRule
Without an object (intransitive)grow up, break up, work out, drift apart, settle downThey take no object: They broke up last year.
Separable (with an object)let (someone) down, call (someone) up, bring (someone) upThe noun can go in the middle or after: let Ana down / let down Ana. With a pronoun it always goes in the middle: let her down.
Inseparable and three-partlook after, run into, get along with, look up to, put up with, fall out with, keep up withNever separated: I look up to her. I can't put up with it.

Many have more than one meaning: work out = turn out well / exercise / calculate. Learn each phrasal verb inside a complete sentence.

watch.why: With a pronoun, the pronoun goes between the verb and the particle.

watch.wrong: They broke up me last year.
watch.right: They broke up with me last year.
watch.why: With an object you need with: break up with someone.

watch.wrong: I can't put up it anymore.
watch.right: I can't put up with it anymore.
watch.why: Put up with has three parts: it is not separated.

watch.wrong: I get along him very well.
watch.right: I get along with him very well.
watch.why: Get along with + person; forgetting with is a common mistake.

learn.title: Phrasal verbs for relationships (relationships and contact)

words.example: I fell out with my cousin over money.
We argued, but we made up the next day.
After college, we just drifted apart.
I lost touch with her when she moved abroad.

words.example: I got back in touch with an old classmate on social media.
Let's keep in touch after the course ends.
I get along with all my colleagues.
I've always looked up to my older brother.
Don't worry; I won't let you down.
You can always count on me.
She broke up with her boyfriend last month.
They settled down and bought a house.
I usually hang out with my friends on Fridays.
I can't put up with rude people.
I bumped into an old friend at the supermarket.

learn.title: both, neither, either and each other
learn.html:
They are used to talk about two people or things at the same time.

StructureExampleNotes
be + bothWe're both fans of the same band.With be, both goes after the verb.
both + other verbWe both work in design.With other verbs, both goes before.
both of us / themBoth of us like hiking.As a subject; verb in the plural.
neither of us / themNeither of us likes getting up early.Already negative: the verb is affirmative. Singular verb (in informal English a plural is also heard).
either ofI don't think either of them is right.«Either of the two»; used in negative sentences or questions.
both … and / neither … norShe's both kind and funny. He's neither rude nor arrogant.Parallel structures.
each other / one anotherThey've known each other for years.Reciprocal action (with each other). It is not the same as themselves.

watch.wrong: Neither of us doesn't like horror films.
watch.right: Neither of us likes horror films.
watch.why: Neither is already negative: don't add another negation.
After of, use the object pronoun: us, them.

watch.wrong: They love themselves (= se quieren el uno al otro).
watch.why: Reciprocity = each other; themselves is reflexive.
Both goes before the main verb.

learn.title: Softening comments (softeners)
learn.html:
In an English conversation, direct criticism sounds harsh. To sound natural and polite, soften with these words:

  • a bit / a little (bit) / kind of / sort of — She's a bit odd. It's kind of weird.
  • I guess / I think / I suppose — I guess that's OK.
  • probably / maybe — He's probably just tired.
  • just — She's just a bit shy.
  • in a way — It's a relief in a way.
  • though (at the end) — He's nice. He talks a lot, though.
  • I wouldn't say… / not exactly the most… — I wouldn't say he's lazy, but… / She's not exactly the most patient person.
  • deep down — He's a bit rough, but deep down he's kind.

A falling intonation and a friendly tone also soften what you say. Don't pile them all into one sentence.

write.prompt: Write a text of 180 to 250 words about an important friendship in your life: how you met, what the person is like, how the relationship has changed and why it is special. Opening example: My oldest friend, who I met at secondary school, is …

Without repeating the pronoun inside the relative clause
Between 180 and 250 words, in paragraphs
write.model:
My oldest friend, who I met at secondary school, is called Daniela. We were sitting next to each other on the first day of class, both of us nervous and a bit lost, and we got along with each other straight away. She is the kind of person whose laugh fills the room, and she has always been the one who organizes everything, which drives me crazy sometimes, though I admire it.

Over the years our friendship has changed. When we went to different universities, we nearly drifted apart, because she moved to Guadalajara, where I had never lived, and I stayed in Mexico City. Neither of us wanted to lose the friendship, so we decided to keep in touch by sending voice messages, which became a kind of ritual. A message sent on Sunday night always started my week well.

Now we both have jobs and busy lives, and we see each other only a few times a year. Still, I guess nothing has really changed. Neither of us feels the need to explain anything, and the woman standing at the airport with a huge smile is the same girl I met at fourteen. That is why she is so special to me: she knows me better than anyone, and she still makes me laugh.

write.prompt: Write an email of 180 to 250 words to a friend you lost touch with: greet them, tell them why you drifted apart (without blaming), update them on your life and suggest meeting up. Opening example: Hi Sofía, I know it's been a long time since we last talked, but …

checklist: Use lose touch, get back in touch or keep in touch
2 relative clauses (one non-defining, with commas)
A reduced clause
Both of us / each other / neither of us
Soften difficult things (I guess, a bit, in a way, though)
A concrete suggestion to meet (Would you like to…? We could…)
Friendly tone and an appropriate closing (Take care, Best wishes)
Between 180 and 250 words
write.model:
Hi Sofía,

I know it's been a long time since we last talked, but I have been thinking about you a lot lately, and I decided it was time to get back in touch.

I guess we both let life get in the way. When you moved to Monterrey, where you started your new job, I was finishing my degree, and neither of us had much free time. We lost touch little by little, and in a way it was nobody's fault. I'm a bit sorry that I didn't call you more often, though I know you understand.

Let me tell you what's new. I'm working at a small design company, which is quite close to my flat, and I have adopted a dog called Canela, a puppy rescued from the street last spring. My brother, who you always liked, is getting married next year. We have a lot to catch up on, and I would love to hear about your life, too.

Would you like to meet up one weekend? We could have coffee in Coyoacán, the neighborhood where we used to hang out. If you're in town in December, we could even have dinner. Both of us love tacos, so it's an easy decision!

I hope we can see each other soon and keep in touch from now on. Take care, and call me whenever you can.

Best wishes,
Laura

reading.title: The Friends We Keep
reading.intro: Read the article about how to make friends in a new city and answer.
paragraphs: When Marisol Vega moved from Puebla to Barcelona at the age of twenty-six, she knew exactly one person in the whole city: her cousin Iván, who had lived there for years. "I thought I would never make friends," she says, laughing. "I had left behind a group of people I'd grown up with, and I couldn't imagine replacing them."

Her first months were lonely. Marisol worked long hours at a design studio, a place where nobody seemed to have time for small talk. She often called her old friends, but the time difference and their busy schedules meant that conversations became shorter and less frequent. "We didn't fall out or anything," she explains. "We just started to drift apart, which was painful because I had always taken those friendships for granted."

Everything changed when she signed up for a pottery class recommended by a colleague. The people attending the class were mostly strangers, yet within weeks she was hanging out with two of them, Jun and Danielle, whose sense of humor matched hers. Both of them had moved to Barcelona alone, and neither of them spoke much Spanish at first, so all three were building a new life from scratch. "We were all looking for the same thing," Marisol says. "We just needed someone to say yes to a coffee."

Today, Marisol's circle includes people from six countries. She admits that not every relationship has worked out, although most of them have become an important part of her daily life. A flatmate she shared an apartment with for a year turned out to be rather possessive about the kitchen, and after a heated argument they stopped speaking. "It was kind of a relief, in a way," she says, "though I still feel a bit guilty."

Researchers studying adult friendship say Marisol's experience is common. People who move to a new city usually need roughly fifty hours of shared time before they consider someone a casual friend, and about two hundred hours before that person becomes a close one. Friendship, in other words, is not a matter of luck; it is a matter of time.

Marisol's advice for anyone starting over? "Don't wait for friendships to happen. Join something, say yes to invitations, and be patient with yourself. And if you lose touch with an old friend, send a message. I got back in touch with my best friend from school last year, and it was as if no time had passed."

Carla! Wow, it's been what, ten years? We completely lost touch after I moved away.
At least ten. I looked for you online last month, but I couldn't find you.
I deleted my account ages ago. Anyway, how's everyone? How's Marcos, the guy who used to sit next to us in math?
Marcos? He's married now, and both of his kids go to my daughter's school. Neither of them likes math, funnily enough.
Ha! Some things never change. And what about Ximena, your old roommate?
We fell out a couple of years after college, but we made up last spring. We get along better than ever now, which is kind of surprising.
That's great. I always looked up to her. Listen, let's not lose touch again. Can I get your number?
Of course. And come for dinner on Saturday. A few friends from college are coming, so it'll be a proper reunion.
I'd love to, though I might be a little late. I'm flying back from Monterrey that afternoon.
No problem. Come whenever you can. Oh, and bring your guitar, which everybody still remembers!
Ha, I haven't played in years, but I guess I could try.
